title: Dressing
heading: Kitsuke: putting it on
intro: A flat robe gets its <q>final fit and shape</q> only in the dressing, called kitsuke {4:p.11}.

labels.title: Taught and certified
body: Kimono academies spread across Japan after the war {4:p.77}, issuing <q>certificates after the completion of certain courses</q> {4:p.78}.
In a 2006 survey of 128 women students at one university, 8.6 per cent could put on a kimono themselves {27:p.774}.

labels.title: Left over right
body: Furisode magazines begin with the under-kimono and end with the obi knot {4:p.72}. The robe is <q>always draped from the left side over to the right</q> {4:p.69}.
The other way round <q>is now associated with death and the afterlife</q> {4:p.70}.

labels.title: Ohashori
body: The extra length becomes <q>the fold of fabric beneath the obi</q> {4:p.71}.
In a yukata study of nine young women, the fold slipped less when the cord was tied at the top of the hip bone than at the waist {19:p.81}.

labels.title: Where the pressure falls
body: In a study of nine young women, clothing pressure was highest at the obi's upper edge, near the armpit {21:p.53}.
Of 333 graduating students in kimono, about eight in ten felt it two to three times as constricting as Western clothes {21:p.56}.

labels.title: Cord, sash and knot
body: Magazines set the obi-jime <q>in the middle of the obi</q>, add an obi-age <q>to complete the ensemble</q> {4:p.71}, and tie the knot <q>facing the wearer's back</q> {4:p.71}.

cues.show: As you walk towards the figure, ask who teaches this. Becke traces a wave of books in the nineteen-seventies on the correct way to wear kimono. One school opened in 1964 and, Becke notes, runs five academies in Japan's biggest cities.

The first layer goes on. In one Japanese case study, a professional dressing of a furisode used sixteen separate items: padding, under-layers, cords, a board, an obi pillow. Together they weighed about three kilograms, nearly four times a sweater and jeans.
Left over right is old. Becke traces it to a clothing code of the year 718, which followed Chinese fashion.
The fold at the waist is easily disturbed. In the yukata study, a bow made kneeling on the floor shifted it most; a standing bow, least.
Women today tie the obi high, from under the bust to the waist. About a century ago, cords and obi sat low, at the hip bones.
The knot is tied last, at the back. Walk round and look.

claims.text: Kitsuke gives the final fit and shape.
claims.quote: The kitsuke is of great importance as it provides the final fit and shape of the garment.
claims.scope: Becke; general

claims.text: Kimono academies spread across Japan after the war.
claims.quote: These institutions started to operate all over Japan in the post-war period
claims.scope: Becke, citing Dalby 2001: 119-121 and Goldstein-Gidoni 1999: 352

claims.text: Academies issue certificates for finished courses.
claims.quote: issuing certificates after the completion of certain courses
claims.scope: kimono academies

claims.text: Only 8.6% of 128 women students could put on a kimono themselves; 35.9% a yukata.
claims.quote: 日本では着物8.6％（11/128 人），ゆかた35.9％（46/128 人）が自分自身で着ることができる
claims.scope: Tr. "in Japan 8.6% (11/128) could put on a kimono and 35.9% (46/128) a yukata by themselves". 128 Otsuma Women's University students, July 2006.

claims.text: The Japanese survey: 128 students of Otsuma Women's University, July 2006.
claims.quote: 日本では2006 年７月に大妻女子大学生128 名
claims.scope: Tr.: "in Japan, 128 students of Otsuma Women's University in July 2006". Added by verifier.

claims.text: Magazine dressing runs from the nagajuban to the final obi knot.
claims.quote: from putting on the nagajuban (under-kimono) to the final tying of the obi knot
claims.scope: furisode; magazine kitsuke columns. Only the first and last steps are ordered in this source

claims.text: The kimono is draped from the left side over to the right.
claims.quote: without exception always draped from the left side over to the right
claims.scope: furisode; what the publications show

claims.text: Wrapping the other way is linked to death.
claims.quote: draping the garment the opposite way is now associated with death and the afterlife
claims.scope: Becke, citing Dalby 2001: 170 and Suzuki 2004

claims.text: Left over right goes back to the Yōrō Clothing Code of 718, in Chinese fashion.
claims.quote: stated that all robes, in Chinese fashion, should be fitted with the left side over the right
claims.scope: the sentence's subject is 'The Yōrō Clothing Code which was implemented in 718'; Becke, citing Dalby 2001: 27-28

claims.text: The ohashori is a fold of fabric beneath the obi.
claims.quote: the creation of an ohashori, the fold of fabric beneath the obi
claims.scope: furisode; magazine convention

claims.text: Ohashori slippage was smaller with the cord at the top of the iliac crest (7.1 cm) than at the waist (8.0 cm).
claims.quote: 腰紐をウエストで締めた時（8.0±2.9cm）に比べて，腸骨稜上縁高で締めた時（7.1±2.5cm）の方が，着崩れ量は有意に少なかった
claims.scope: Tr. "compared with tying the koshihimo at the waist (8.0±2.9 cm), slippage was significantly smaller when tied at the top of the iliac crest (7.1±2.5 cm)". Yukata; 9 women aged 21-23; after 10 repetitions of movements.

claims.text: Seated bowing produced the most ohashori slippage, the standing bow the least.
claims.quote: おはしょりの着崩れ量は立礼＜立ち座り＜一連の動作＜座礼となり
claims.scope: Tr. "ohashori slippage: standing bow < standing and sitting < series of movements < seated bow". Same 9 subjects, yukata.

claims.text: Clothing pressure was highest at the upper edge of the obi, especially at the armpit.
claims.quote: the clothing pressure was high at the upper edge of obi, especially in the axially region
claims.scope: authors' English abstract ('axially' as printed; the text layer reads 'especialy', the page image 'especially'); 9 subjects; 'young women'

claims.text: About 80% of 333 graduating students felt kimono pressure 2-3 times that of Western clothes.
claims.quote: 和服の圧迫感は洋服の2倍から3倍と回答した者が全体の約8割であった
claims.scope: Tr. "about 80% answered that the feeling of pressure in kimono was two to three times that of Western clothes". Kyoto Women's University graduation, March 2005; 71% wore hakama.

claims.text: The 333 were students who attended their graduation in March 2005 in furisode, hōmongi or hakama.
claims.quote: 平成17年3月に京都女子大学の卒業式で振袖や訪問着，袴を着て参列した333人の学生
claims.scope: Tr.: "333 students who attended the Kyoto Women's University graduation in March 2005 in furisode, hōmongi or hakama". Added by verifier.

claims.text: Magazines place the obi-jime in the middle of the obi and add an obi-age to complete the ensemble.
claims.quote: placement in the middle of the obi, and the addition of an obi-age (obi cloth) to complete the ensemble
claims.scope: furisode; magazine convention. Not an ordered step

claims.text: The obi knot faces the wearer's back.
claims.quote: The obi is dominantly tied in an elaborate manner, with the knot facing the wearer’s back.
claims.scope: furisode; magazine convention

claims.text: The 1970s brought a wave of books on the correct way to wear kimono.
claims.quote: The 1970s saw an increase in literature on kimono which aimed to educate the general public on the correct way of wearing kimono
claims.scope: Becke, citing Dalby 2001: 114-121

claims.text: One school opened in 1964 and runs five academies in Japan's biggest cities.
claims.quote: The institution started operating in 1964 and currently manages five academies which operate in the biggest cities throughout Japan
claims.scope: Sōdō Reihō Kimono Gakuin; Becke, from the school's website, via Assmann 2008

claims.text: The women's outfits were put on by one certified professional dresser; one outfit was furisode with fukuro obi.
claims.quote: 女子の着物の着付けは，資格を持った専門家１名が行い
claims.scope: Tr.: "the women's kimono were dressed by one qualified professional". The same page lists the outfits: 振袖に袋帯を文庫に結ぶ (furisode with fukuro obi tied in bunko). Lecture; case study. Added by verifier.

claims.text: One professional dressing of a furisode with fukuro obi listed sixteen components (only one is a board, maeita).
claims.quote: 胸増し綿＋ガーゼ＋肌襦袢＋長襦袢＋帯下締め＋長着＋第１腰紐＋きものベルト＋第２腰紐＋伊達締め＋前板＋帯＋紐＋帯枕＋帯揚げ＋帯〆
claims.scope: Tr. "chest padding cotton + gauze + hadajuban + nagajuban + under-obi tie + kimono + 1st koshihimo + kimono belt + 2nd koshihimo + datejime + front board + obi + cord + obi pillow + obiage + obijime". One professional dressing of a fukuro-obi furisode; a lecture, case study.

claims.text: That outfit weighed about 3 kg, 3.75 times a sweater and jeans.
claims.quote: 総重量は約3kgと洋服（セータ＋ジーンズ）の3.75倍の負担となりました
claims.scope: Tr. "total weight about 3 kg, a load 3.75 times Western clothes (sweater + jeans)". Case study; lecture.

claims.text: Women's obi are tied from under the bust to the waist.
claims.quote: 女子の帯はアンダーバストからウエストにかけて結びます
claims.scope: Tr. "women's obi are tied from under the bust to the waist". Present-day; lecture.

claims.text: Until about 100 years ago, cords and obi were tied low, at the hip bones.
claims.quote: 100 年程前まで，腰紐を腰骨のあたりに締める，骨盤の張り出したところに帯を締める
claims.scope: Tr. "until about 100 years ago, koshihimo were tied around the hip bones and the obi where the pelvis protrudes". Sato and Tamura, from secondary sources.

dropped: Every dressing step between the under-kimono and the obi knot as a rule: Becke orders only the first and last; the sixteen-item list is one professional's dressing in a case study (source 20).
How long dressing takes when women dress themselves: only an expert's 5-7 minutes for summer layers (source 24) was found; not used.
That a high obi raises stress markers: the English quote read (source 18 p.126) covers only the men's low position; left out.
